primary_meaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, feet most commonly symbolize a person's 'walk'—that is, one's conduct, moral direction, and course of life. To have one's feet on a right path, kept from stumbling, or set upon a rock is read as living faithfully and obediently before God, while straying or slipping feet represent sin and moral failure.
primary_basis: Psalm 119:105 ('a lamp to my feet and a light to my path')
Psalm 1:1 (the way/walk of the righteous vs. the wicked)
Proverbs 4:26-27 ('ponder the path of your feet')
Psalm 40:2 ('set my feet upon a rock')
Psalm 121:3 ('he will not let your foot be moved')
Proverbs 6:18 ('feet that make haste to run to evil')
Ephesians 6:15 (feet shod with readiness of the gospel of peace)
Luke 1:79 ('to guide our feet into the way of peace')

alternatives.meaning: Feet as the emblem of the messenger who proclaims good news—the 'beautiful feet' of gospel heralds and evangelists.
Feet as a symbol of dominion, victory, and subjection—enemies placed 'under the feet' of God, Christ, or his people.
basis: Genesis 3:15 (crushing the serpent's head, often linked)

alternatives.meaning: Feet (especially footwashing) as a symbol of humility, servanthood, and cleansing from daily defilement—Christ washing the disciples' feet as the model of humble service and ongoing sanctification.
Sitting or falling at someone's feet as a posture of discipleship, worship, and submission to a teacher or to Christ.
The foot treading on land as a sign of taking possession or claiming inheritance/territory.

Feet in visionary imagery as a symbol of judgment, stability, or divine character—e.g., Christ's feet like burnished bronze, the iron-and-clay feet of Nebuchadnezzar's statue as fragile kingdoms, treading the winepress of wrath.
Feet as the humble but necessary members of the body of Christ, teaching mutual dependence within the church.

notes: Feet do not carry one single settled symbolic meaning in Christian interpretation; the meaning is strongly context-dependent. The 'walk of life' sense is arguably the broadest and most frequently invoked in devotional and homiletical use, but the messenger motif (Isa 52:7/Rom 10:15), dominion motif (Ps 110:1), and humility/footwashing motif (John 13) are each robust, well-attested strands with their own liturgical and doctrinal traditions (e.g., Maundy Thursday footwashing; christological use of Ps 110). Any claim that feet have one fixed symbolic meaning across Scripture would exceed the recognizable consensus, which treats the symbol as a cluster of related but distinct usages.
